bullets: ‘Yes! and the bedpost was his own. The bed was his own, the room was his own.’: repetition of ‘own’: relief, second chance.
‘I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future!’: repeating his vow.
‘I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a school-boy. I am as giddy as a drunken man.’
He laughs: ‘a splendid laugh, a most illustrious laugh’: the first of ‘a long line of brilliant laughs’.
Bright morning: ‘No fog, no mist… Golden sunlight’.
Sends a boy to buy the prize turkey for the Cratchits anonymously, laughing at the thought of it.
Meets the charity collector and whispers a large donation, with ‘back-payments’ included.
Goes to church, walks the streets, pats children on the head, gives to beggars: rejoining the community.
Goes to Fred’s: ‘Wonderful party, wonderful games, wonderful unanimity, wonderful happiness!’
Pretends to be angry with Bob for being late, then raises his salary: comic reversal.
‘Make up the fires, and buy another coal-scuttle before you dot another i, Bob Cratchit!’
‘He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew’.
‘to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father’.
Some people laughed at the change; ‘his own heart laughed: and that was quite enough for him’.
‘it was always said of him, that he knew how to keep Christmas well’.

callouts.p: It shows that change is possible and joyful, models the behaviour Dickens wants from readers, and mirrors Stave 1 so the change is measurable.

exam.q: Explore how Dickens presents Scrooge’s happiness in this extract (Stave 5). (20 marks)
exam.tip: Compare implicitly with Stave 1’s language even in part (a): it shows understanding.

mistakes.r: It is a moral fable; the exaggeration is deliberate and joyful, modelling change for readers.
mistakes.w: The change is unbelievable so Dickens failed.

quotes.q: I am as light as a feather
a great many back-payments are included in it

summary: Stave 5 shows the transformed Scrooge on Christmas morning: joyful, generous and reconnected, reversing every encounter of Stave 1; learn the key moments and how Dickens uses comedy, repetition and the cyclical structure to show change.

terms.d: The ending that resolves the story’s problems.
A humorous scene where expectations are overturned (Bob’s pay rise).
